summary: Specifies conventions for using the NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite with the SSH Transport Layer Protocol and the SSH Authentication Protocol. It applies to US National Security Systems using SSH and is also appropriate for other US Government systems with high-value information. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A list of approved locks for remote logins in the most sensitive government systems.

questions: how does ssh key exchange work
subtitle: NSA-approved cryptographic algorithms for securing government SSH connections.

tldr.problem: US Government systems need to use cryptographically strong algorithms for SSH that meet national security requirements and are resistant to future quantum computing threats.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies which algorithms, key sizes, and configuration options from the NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite must be used with SSH for key exchange, authentication, and encryption.
tldr.outcome: Government agencies can deploy SSH with standardized, approved cryptographic algorithms designed to protect sensitive communications.

today: RFC 9212 is an Informational RFC providing authoritative guidance on applying the NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite to SSH. It is not itself an Internet Standard, but compliant SSH implementations in US Government systems must follow its requirements.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how to use the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite with the Secure Shell protocol (SSH). The CNSA Suite is a set of cryptographic algorithms approved by the United States National Security Agency for protecting government information systems.

The RFC applies to all US National Security Systems that use SSH, and also to other US Government systems handling high-value information. It draws on earlier RFCs that documented how individual CNSA components integrate with SSH, providing a single authoritative guide for proper configuration.

The CNSA Suite was established to provide flexibility during the transition to quantum-resistant cryptography. Rather than forcing agencies to make two major cryptographic transitions in a short timeframe, CNSA allows gradual evolution while maintaining security standards today.
sections.eli5: The government needs secure ways for computers to talk to each other. The NSA approves specific locks that are strong enough for sensitive work.

sections.title: Approved Algorithms
sections.content:
The CNSA Suite for SSH requires specific algorithms in four areas:

Key Exchange: Three algorithms are approved: ecdh-sha2-nistp384 (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman using the NIST P-384 curve with SHA-384), and two Diffie-Hellman variants using SHA-512 with 15- and 16-bit group parameters. The RFC states that SHA-384-based algorithms SHOULD be preferred, though SHA-512 MAY be used.

Authentication: Two public key algorithms are approved: ecdsa-sha2-nistp384 (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) and rsa-sha2-512 (RSA with SHA-512). For RSA, the key modulus must be either 3072 or 4096 bits; other sizes are rejected.

Encryption and Integrity: Only AEAD_AES_256_GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode with 256-bit keys) is permitted for both encryption and message authentication. All 16 octets of the authentication tag must be used, and the invocation counter must be properly incremented modulo 2^64 with no repeats.
sections.eli5: The approved locks use three types of math: elliptic curves (strong and modern), big prime numbers (Diffie-Hellman), and AES encryption. The government says which specific versions to use.

sections.title: Algorithm Negotiation
sections.content:
When a client and server establish an SSH connection, they exchange SSH_MSG_KEXINIT packets to negotiate which algorithms to use. The RFC specifies that all algorithm choices must result in the approved combinations above.

The kex_algorithms field in KEXINIT must contain one of the three approved key exchange algorithms; RFC 9142's diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 must NOT be used. Similarly, the server and client must agree on one of the two approved public key algorithms for authentication.

For encryption and MAC algorithms, implementations may advertise either the explicit AEAD_AES_256_GCM as both encryption and MAC, or use the OpenSSH-specific aes256-gcm@openssh.com notation with an empty MAC list. Both achieve the same result: AES-256-GCM for both confidentiality and integrity.
sections.eli5: When computers start talking, they say which locks they'll use. Both sides must pick from the approved list, or the connection stops.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two key exchange methods. With ECDH, the client sends an ephemeral public key and the server responds with its ephemeral key, the server's permanent host key, and a signature over the exchange hash. With Diffie-Hellman, the flow is similar but uses discrete logarithm parameters instead of elliptic curves.

Critical to CNSA compliance: ephemeral private keys must be used exactly once and destroyed immediately after the key exchange. Shared secrets must be zeroized immediately after use. This prevents any reuse of exchange values that could compromise security.

Server authentication uses a digital signature on the exchange hash. The server's public key must be validated by the client before accepting the signature—either through certificates or another secure mechanism. The RFC explicitly forbids the Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU) model, where clients accept unverified keys from servers they have never contacted before.

User authentication follows RFC 4252 and should be done with public keys (using the same approved algorithms as server authentication). Password authentication is permitted if passwords have sufficient entropy, but other methods including 'none' are not allowed. If RSA is used for user authentication, keys must be 3072 or 4096 bits.
sections.eli5: During login, computers prove they are who they say using math and signatures. Keys get thrown away after use. Trusting a stranger's key is forbidden.

sections.title: Encryption, Integrity, and Rekeying
sections.content:
SSH binary packets use AES-256-GCM for both encryption and authentication. The GCM mode produces a 16-octet authentication tag that serves as SSH's data integrity check; all 16 octets must be used. The invocation counter (used to prevent cipher stream reuse) increments modulo 2^64 and must never repeat.

RFC 4253 permits servers and clients to rekey—to exchange new SSH_MSG_KEXINIT packets and establish new algorithms. However, the CNSA Suite requires that cipher algorithms remain the same during rekeying. The same AES-256-GCM configuration must continue; no algorithm switching is allowed.
sections.eli5: Every message gets scrambled with a strong cipher and a checksum. When computers refresh their shared secret, they keep using the same cipher.
